cim: How CERN Earns Trust at Scale
cim_eredeti: How CERN Earns Trust at Scale
szoveg_eredeti:
Understanding how one of the world’s most enduring and successful large-scale science collaborations has made its work credible can help Europe build trustworthy infrastructure for artificial intelligence in science.

More than 300 feet beneath the mountain foothills, farmland, and quiet border towns between Switzerland and France, superconducting magnets in a 17-mile ring are kept at a temperature below −450 degrees Fahrenheit. Inside the ring, two beams of protons accelerate in opposite directions to nearly the speed of light before colliding head-on at four different points along the path. This machine is the Large Hadron Collider, the most powerful particle accelerator in the world, designed to recreate the universe’s earliest moments and help answer fundamental questions about how it all began.

Along the beams’ route, in caverns built at the collision points, are four particle detectors: ATLAS, CMS, ALICE, and LHCb. Each is its own separate experiment, designed and run by a different international collaboration. It was two of these, ATLAS and CMS, that independently confirmed the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012. The scale of these collaborations is hard to grasp—in 2025, the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics recognized 13,508 coauthors from more than 70 countries for a decade of results across all four experiments.

While the particles race underground, control rooms above monitor the machines and collisions, coordinating the efforts of thousands of researchers in real time. These rooms, and the shared vigilance and collaboration they make possible, are fundamental to the work done at the institution behind all this: CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. A citadel for physicists and a striking example of cooperative scientific governance, CERN has famously produced radical discoveries in subatomic physics along with spillovers like the World Wide Web.

Despite operating as a coalition of 25 member states, with 11 more holding associate status, CERN is known for its stability, even in the face of global power struggles. So it’s no surprise that as Europe has grappled with strategizing around artificial intelligence, one guiding metaphor for a “European way” has been “CERN for AI.”

Europe’s push to develop its own approach to AI governance arrives as the technology has become an explicit front in the geopolitics of scientific research. In initiatives such as the United States’ Genesis Mission, launched in November 2025, AI in science is framed explicitly as an issue of competitiveness and sovereignty, a way to secure scientific leadership, innovation capacity, and strategic autonomy in an era of intensifying US–China AI rivalry. Across these strategies, the central assumption is clear: Whoever controls the foundations of AI, including compute, data, and frontier models, will increasingly shape the pace and direction of discovery—and the future of science itself.

Europe has been a leader in AI-related scientific output, but it has weaker access to large-scale compute, foundational models, and platform ecosystems. In October 2025, the European Commission adopted the European Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Science as part of its bid to ensure leadership and competitiveness. But rather than embracing an all-out race for speed and scale, the strategy anchors Europe’s approach to AI development in public values, accountability, and trustworthiness: “A European approach to a safe, sustainable, human-centric and trustworthy AI in science is a strategic opportunity in the rapidly changing geopolitical environment,” it reads.

The idea of a “CERN for AI” dates back to 2017; since then, it has circulated as a strategic metaphor, claimed by different actors to mean very different things. In February 2025, the European Commission president invoked CERN to describe Europe’s ambition to build a coordinated, public infrastructure for AI. That grew into the flagship initiative of the Strategy for AI in Science: RAISE, or the Resource for Artificial Intelligence Science in Europe, with an initial €107 million in funding from Horizon Europe.

Europe’s push to develop its own approach to AI governance arrives as the technology has become an explicit front in the geopolitics of scientific research.

Like CERN, RAISE is transnational and designed to do what no single nation can achieve alone. But unlike CERN, it will not take shape as a single monumental site. Instead, it is being built as a virtual institute with a distributed network, weaving together Europe’s supercomputers, data hubs, and AI factories into a shared infrastructure. In the Commission’s framing, its aim is to support Europe’s ambition to become an “AI Continent” while remaining aligned with European commitments to ethics, accountability, safety, and human rights.

RAISE and related AI-for-science initiatives are being framed in a geopolitical register, but in practice they are also institutional reforms of how science is structured and performed. Embedding AI into research infrastructures reshapes the everyday craft of science: how problems are framed, how evidence is produced, how results are validated, and how uncertainty is handled. As these new infrastructures solidify, so too do the norms and forms of authority that will govern science in the years to come, often before those arrangements are made explicit or subject to debate.

Now, while these choices are still open, is the ideal moment to really think through what it means to build a distributed AI infrastructure for science, and what must be built into that infrastructure to ensure it reinforces Europe’s stated commitment to trustworthy AI. I come to this question as an anthropologist and science, technology, and society scholar studying the future of universities and academic work, and how artificial intelligence is now reshaping the whole knowledge-making ecosystem. I spent nearly a decade visiting CERN as part of the Challenge Based Innovation program, working with student teams tackling big societal challenges, inspired by CERN’s science and the people behind it. Seeing CERN up close, I kept returning to a question with colleagues there: What would it mean to bring not just CERN’s technology, but its ethos and methods, to bear on challenges at that scale?

Many “CERN for AI” discussions spotlight CERN’s governance and institutional design. My focus here is different: the everyday practices and shared standards through which CERN makes trust—in its machinery, and in the knowledge it produces—possible. CERN doesn’t offer a blueprint for AI, but it exemplifies elements of scientific infrastructure that are essential yet easily overlooked, including designed visibility of complex systems, shared practices for collective judgment, and careful methods for handling uncertainty.

It is tempting to think of CERN only as a triumph of scale and engineering: a vast complex of accelerators, detectors, and tunnels built to probe the fundamental structure of matter. This image often stands in for “Big Science” more generally, reinforcing the idea that CERN’s primary lesson lies in technical ambition or concentrated resources. But this reading misses what has made CERN historically distinctive and politically durable. From its founding in 1954, in the aftermath of the Second World War, CERN was conceived not simply as a laboratory, but as a political infrastructure for rebuilding European science (and Europe) through cooperation. It was designed to pool resources and research capacity across the borders of its original 12 member states after decades of fragmentation and scientific brain drain. Its founding convention embedded a public, nonmilitary ethos from the outset, explicitly committing the organization to “have no concern with work for military requirements.”
